RESEARCH REGISTER / CHECKED SEPTEMBER 22, 2026 UTC

Every number has a boundary.

Public data can support a useful shortlist. It cannot establish how many additional visitors a place should receive.

How the data were collected

We extracted published aggregate tables from public agency and university reports, then normalized park names and dates into CSV files. No surveys of individuals, device records, names, contact details, or personal locations were collected. All chart values come from these collected tables or their documented calculations.

Each park’s 12 monthly counts is checked against its annual total. Every 2025 selected-park total also matches the university economic report. The 2024 PDF was downloaded; several other reports were readable through indexed public text despite direct-download failures. Those retrieval limitations are disclosed below.

Calculations

Peak-relative visitation
100 × monthly visits / highest monthly count for that park and year. This is an index of seasonal timing, not a percentage of capacity.
Share of annual visits
100 × monthly visits / total visits for the calendar year. Summer totals cover June, July and August.
Year-over-year change
100 × (2025 total / 2024 total − 1). The five-park combined change excludes Rockin’ River Ranch, which was not open in January 2024.
Recommendation method
Editorial screening using the seasonal pattern, attraction type, published access and missing evidence. No hidden weights or numerical “opportunity score.” September Cottonwood, summer Jerome, and off-peak Fort Verde are proposed experiments, not proven optimal choices.

Missing data, bias and uncertainty

  • Selection bias: six parks were chosen for proximity and comparable public reporting. Private attractions, tribal destinations and many community businesses are outside the comparison.
  • Capacity is unknown: fewer visits do not prove empty parking, available rooms, ecological headroom or enough staff.
  • Timing is descriptive: two years, unequal month lengths and unknown opening-day changes limit comparison. Weather, events and closures can drive observed differences.
  • Geographies differ: park counts, 50-mile spending areas, hotel study markets and Sedona residents cannot be combined as if they described the same population.
  • No causal claim: side trips may extend travel or shift visits without reducing Sedona crowding. Neither campaign effects nor additional spending can be predicted from these records.
  • Receiving-community voice: no comparable local sentiment series was collected for candidate communities. Consultation is a condition of the recommendations.

Source register

1–2. Monthly park visitation

Arizona State Parks Revenue and Attendance Monthly Reports, compiled by NAU’s Arizona Hospitality Research and Resource Center. Calendar years 2024 and 2025, January–December. Units: park visits. Six selected parks, 144 observations.

2024 original PDF ↗ · 2025 original PDF ↗ · Arizona tourism report archive ↗

The 2024 PDF was downloaded and parsed with text extraction. The 2025 table was available through indexed source text, but direct download returned 404 during collection. Its six annual totals were cross-checked against Table 2 of source 3. No missing month was imputed. Rockin’ River Ranch’s reported January 2024 zero is retained with a “not yet open” flag, and shown as a dash in the heatmap. The park opened in February 2024. Totals in these tables are counts of visits, not unique individuals.

3. Visitor spending around state parks

Dari Duval and Claudia Montanía, University of Arizona Cooperative Extension, 2025 Economic Contributions & Impacts of Arizona State Parks, published June 2026. Calendar year 2025; nominal USD. Tables 35 and 44 report category spending and direct totals associated with non-local visitors.

Original report ↗ · Publication page ↗

The study uses a 2025 visitor survey (10,693 observations across 30 parks; 8,600 with usable expenditure information). Spending concerns activity in and within 50 miles of each park. Non-local means visitors from over 50 miles away. Our chart uses direct spending, not indirect or induced effects. Source category totals can differ from published direct totals by $1,000 through rounding. We do not sum parks into a regional windfall or calculate per-new-visitor revenue. Park-level sampling uncertainty is not quantified here.

4. Sedona resident feedback

National Community Survey, City of Sedona, 2024. Fieldwork September 9–October 28, 2024. We use the weighted probability sample, excluding the separate open-participation results. Overall sample: 551; response rate: 20%; reported overall margin of error: up to ±4 percentage points at 95% confidence. The item-specific sample size was not separately published in the extracted table.

Original survey report ↗ · City survey archive ↗

Question: “In the future, how much of a role would you like to see tourism have in Sedona’s economy?” Less: 49%; same: 45%; more: 6%. Nonresponse and demographic coverage may affect estimates. These views do not measure support for side-trip promotion, and cannot be assigned to Cottonwood, Jerome or Camp Verde.

5. Hotel-market context

City of Sedona Tourism Program, October 2025 Lodging and Spending Reports, STR hotel review, PDF page 4. Six monthly observations: August–October 2025 for Sedona+ and Village of Oak Creek+. Occupancy is rooms sold / rooms available; ADR is average daily room rate in USD, not total trip cost.

Original lodging report ↗

Read the October 2025 Hotel Review panel; the PDF also contains older narrative text, which is not used. The sample note (as of April 2025) lists 21 of 44 Sedona+ hotels and 6 of 14 Village of Oak Creek+ hotels reporting. A June closure for renovation reduced Sedona+ supply. These vendor-defined markets do not measure accommodation availability in our candidate towns. We omit short-term rentals because the report uses multiple geographic and vendor definitions; no values are substituted for missing candidate-town capacity.

6. Attractions, access and operating constraints

Official park pages checked September 22, 2026. Hours describe the published current offer, not a reconstructed 2024–2025 operating history. This study does not provide live alerts or verified driving times.

  • Dead Horse Ranch ↗ — Cottonwood nature, camping and river setting.
  • Jerome ↗ — Douglas Mansion museum; daily opening listed.
  • Fort Verde ↗ — historic buildings, exhibitions and event calendar.
  • Rockin’ River Ranch ↗ — Friday–Sunday operation listed; last entry 4 p.m.
  • Arizona State Parks FY2024 annual report ↗ — February 2024 opening of Rockin’ River Ranch.
  • Verde Shuttle route ↗ — connection between central Cottonwood and Sedona, not direct park access.
  • Arizona State Parks summer guide ↗ — experience and seasonal context.
